title: The Cholas and their Coinage
html:
THE CHOLAS AND THEIR COINAGE

BY

DIWAN BAHADUR T. DESIKACHARI, B.A., B.L., M.R.A.S.

CENTURIES before the Christian era, the Cholas had established themselves on the coast of Coromandel (Chola mandalam) and enjoyed a civilization not less advanced than that of the Aryan Settlements in the North. They were referred to along with the Keralas and the Pandyas in the Second Rock Edict of the Buddhist Emperor, Asoka, in the third century B.C. The great chronicle of Ceylon, an ancient work in Pali called the Mahavanso, made it the theme of one of its main episodes, the war waged against the Island by the Chola Tamils in the early centuries preceding the Christian era.

Some scholars have advanced the hypothesis that it was a colony of Dravidian merchants who, becoming acquainted with an alphabetic writing derived from the white Pre-Semetic Akkadians north of the Euphrates Valley, brought the script to India, being thus the first to introduce the art of writing into Dravida Desam. There is in the proof that is adduced in support of this hypothesis much that tends to show that the Tamils, as early as the seventh century before the Christian era, had developed such a degree of maritime and commercial enterprise as to tempt them to undertake voyages across the sea to distant countries. The principal port of the Cholas was Kaveripaddinam, situated near the northern mouth of the Kaveri.

The first capital of the Cholas was Uraiyur. probably the oldest portion of the modern Trichinopoly ; and later on they ruled from their capital Jayam-Koṇda-Cholapuram, in the Udaiyarpalayam Taluq of the Trichinopoly District, the relics of whose greatness are still to be seen in an embankment, many miles long, of a ruined reservoir, probably one of the largest in India, and a temple which, even in its present neglected condition, attests to its once magnificent proportions and costly Dravidian architecture. Other places there are too in the same District, which remind us by their names of these ancient rulers, such as Gangai-Koṇda-Cholapuram and Gandarādittam. As the Chola kings grew in power they had their capitals Tanjore, Kumbakonam and Conjivaram and their Viceroys in Rajahmundry in the north and Madura in the South. It is interesting to note that when Samudragupta raided the South about 340 A.D., a Pallava ruled at Kanchi.

In addition to the notice of their existence in the Asoka Edicts and the Mahavanso, before the Christian era, we find allusions to the Cholas, in the Periplus Maris Erithræ in the first century, in Ptolemy's Geography in the second century, in the travels of Hiun Thsang in the seventh century and in the travels of Marco Polo in the thirteenth century of the Christian era. Beyond references to the existence of the Cholas as a ruling power there is nothing in these contemporary records that could help us in the construction of a connected Chola History. Nor do we derive substantial aid from Sanskrit or Tamil writings, which give conflicting accounts the accuracy of which has yet to be confirmed by lithic records which however have so far not taken us earlier than the eighth century A.D. We, no doubt, now and then meet with in the indigenous literature names like Köchengannán and Karikâla. Of these, the latter is reputed to have built the Kaveri embankments, employed forced labour paying them with leather money, thus invoking the anger of the Gods and a dust-storm which destroyed his capital, and probably ruled in the second century of the Christian era. The same name is also mentioned as that of the persecutor of the great Vaishnavite Reformer, Ramanujacharya, who had to flee out of the Chola kingdom and take refuge with the King Vishnu Vardhana. But all these sovereigns have yet to be allotted their proper places in Chola genealogy. The Chola inscriptions and coins which have hitherto come to light relate to a period between the ninth and thirteenth centuries of the Christian era, during which the Cholas rose into great prominence and finally declined, leaving only the numerous South Indian Temples, inscriptions and coins to attest to their greatness. Inscriptions are, however, not wanting to show that the Cholas were a power to be reckoned with even anterior to the eighth century of the Christian era. During the supremacy of that strange race, the Pallavas, the Cholas seem to have occupied but a subordinate position, but had never lost their native virility or a good portion of their inherited dominions.

It is when the history of the Pandyan kings becomes intimately connected with that of the Chola and Sinhalese sovereigns that we begin to have the help of Epigraphy and Numismatics. It is then too that the account in the Mahavanso of the inroads of the Tamils into the island of Ceylon and of the reprisals of the Sinhalese on the mainland come to be matter of lithic record.

Between the ninth and thirteenth centuries of the Christian era the Chola kings, with varying success, attempted to maintain their supremacy over the whole of the Southern Presidency. In order to understand the coins of this period, it is necessary to bear in mind who were the contemporary kings that ruled in different portions of the country over which the Cholas struggled for predominence. There were the Chalukyas of Rajahmundry in the north and the Pallavas who had ruled on the Coromandel coast with Kanchipuram as their capital. From Nellore and the Ghauts to the sea, was the ancient Dravida Desam, or the land of the Tamils, of which the northern portion the Chola Desam, extended from the Kaveri to the Palar; from the Kaveri to Comorin was the Pandya country; and the Chera country comprised all the territory westward as far as the sea. Another race of kings playing a prominent part in the Chola history of this period are the Gangas, who ruled probably from Mukkalingam near Parlakimedi in the Ganjam District. And if to these be added the Sinhalese sovereigns who governed the Island of Ceylon, during the time of the Chola ascendancy in the mainland and the King of Pegu, the tale of sovereignties, with the conquest of which the Chola history mainly deals, would be almost complete.

A fairly reliable genealogy of the Chola soveriegns of this period is now available. Parantaka ruled from A.D. 907 to 949, from Uraiyur and was known as 'Madurantaka' and 'Vira Narayana.' The Jains were numerically strong during his reign but he is also reputed to have built the Kanaka Sabha or the Golden Hall of the Chidambaram Temple, a meritorious act of devotion to Siva, to which more than one Chola sovereign lays claim. No coins of the king have been yet found.

After Parantaka (whose accession was in A.D. 907 and death in A.D. 949) till we come to the time of his great grandson Raja Raja, who ascended the throne in A.D. 985, we meet with the name of no remarkable Chola king. 'Certain inscriptions of Parantaka are of special interest to the student of village institutions by reason of the full details they give of the manner in which local affairs were administered by well organised local committees, or Panchayats exercising administrative and judicial control under royal sanction.' The immediate predecessor of Raja Raja, was the grandson of Parantaka and the son of Gandaraditya. He assumed the title of Madurantaka and was known as Uttama Chola. To this monarch must be assigned, one of the two varieties of coins, bearing the legend 'Uttama Chola' in Grandha characters, and having a seated tiger with a fish. in front of it, the tiger being the dynastic emblem of the Cholas and the fish that of the Pandyas. It was not unnatural that the king who assumed the name 'Madurantaka' 'conqueror of the Pandyan capital Madura,' should adopt on his coins the Pandyan emblem of the fish in token of his sovereignty over the Pandyan country. The other coin of Uttama Chola has the Chera emblem, the bow, in addition to the fish and the tiger and has the legend in Devanagari characters and this coin has to be attributed to a later reign, that of Rajendra I, whose coins bearing the same emblems have the legend in Nagari, 'Sri Rajendrah.' There has always been a tendency in the Dravida country to pay increasing deference to the classical language, Sanskrit; and the period of the currency of the two coins above noticed could be determined by the change (from the Grandha to the Devanagari) in the characters used in inscribing the legend on the coins.

One unique specimen has the legend in old Tamil 'Avanipa Sekaran Cholaha,' with two fishes on the obverse, but without any symbol to indicate that it had a Chola origin. In the Indian Antiquary for 1892, Dr. Hultzsch read the legend as 'Avanipa Sekaran Golaga,' and interpreted it to mean the round coin of 'Avanipa Sekaran,' but he was not quite certain of his reading. The absence of the dynastic emblem of the tiger is not peculiar to this coin alone, for, as will be presently pointed out, many of the coins of Raja Raja do not bear that emblem. It is not improbable that imitating the pronunciation of the Sanskrit 'Cholah' an attempt was made to transcribe the word in Tamil, in order that the legend might sound quite classical. It was unnecessary to show on the coin the Chola's dynastic emblem when the name of the king himself was given, while the two fishes on the obverse, indicated his supremacy in the Pandyan and Chola territories. On the other hand reading the legend as 'Golaga' and interpreting it as a 'round coin' would lead to the assumption that the perfectly superfluous information that the coin was round in shape, was conveyed by the legend, when the roundness of the coin was an obvious index of its shape. And the term 'gola' was itself one which could not have been paraded by a supreme sovereign having regard to its opprobrious significance in the Hindu Law.

After Madurantaka alias Uttama Chola, came by far the greatest of the Chola kings, Raja Raja I, alias Raja Kesari Varma who ascended the throne in A.D. 985. He maintained a large standing army of well disciplined bodyguards, foot soldiers and archers, that was ever in readiness for active service, and with the aid of his valiant troops he quelled the rebellion of Kandalur Salai, subdued the Vengi and Ganga countries, defeated and humbled the Chalukyas, deprived the Pandyas of their splendour, took Ceylon and so distinguished himself. We read in one of his inscriptions, that he was worthy of worship everywhere. From 1001 A.D., he sheathed his sword and cultivated the arts of peace. When he ascended the throne, the Chola kingdom hardly comprised the districts of Trichinopoly and Tanjore and a portion of the district of Coimbatore. Before he died, he had destroyed the Chera fleet, his power extended over the whole of the modern Presidency of Madras, part of Mysore, the Island of Ceylon, the Laccadives and the Maldives. It was he who built the Brihatiswara Temple at Tanjore one of the grandest specimens of Dravidian architecture in Southern India.

Though a great Saiva devotee he seems to have been tolerant of other sects and creeds. A set of twenty one copper plates, preserved now in the University Museum in Leyden in Holland, hence known as the Leyden Grant, records the interesting fact that he granted a village to a Buddhist Vihara at Negapatam, a monastery which was probably on the site of the present St. Joseph's buildings in that town.

The regulations for the levy of taxes and the minuteness with which the land measurements were made indicate the great care bestowed by Raja Raja in the administration of the large empire which he had built up during his reign. From 1011 A.D. his son Rajendra ruled the country along with the father as heir apparent.

The coins of Raja Raja also attest to the extent of his dominions and the length and prosperity of his rule, and throughout the Madras Presidency, we meet with his copper kasu in large numbers. Every itinerant pedlar who barters pepper, turmeric and spices for old copper is able to get together, after a week's labour, a large number of these specimens current more than nine hundred years ago. The commonest of these bear on their obverse a standing human figure clad in regal robes, and on the reverse the same figure seated, with the legend in Devanagari characters, 'Raja Raja' under the right arm. Coins with similar devices and legend occur also, but more rarely, in silver and gold.

The Chola emblem, generally found on seals, is a seated tiger ; on the coins of the later Chola sovereigns, the figure of the seated tiger is found flanked by the fish, the Pandyan emblem and the bow, the Chera emblem. Yet this characteristic Chola device of the tiger is not generally to be found on the coins of Raja Raja. The only known instance in which the dynastic device is figured on his issues is a coin in impure silver, on the obverse of which is the typical squatting human figure above referred to with a seated tiger flanked by lamps and surmounted by a parasol, with on the reverse the seated tiger, the fish and the bow respectively, the Chola, Pandya and Chera emblems. On the other hand, the standing and seated human figures adverted to already are familiar symbols of the Sinhalese sovereigns of Ceylon, so much so that Raja Raja's coins are usually referred to as those of the Ceylon type. The adoption of this Ceylon type by Raja Raja, the greatest monarch of his age, must be of real significance. Might it not be that, to commemorate his victory over the king of Ceylon, and publish his supremacy in countries even beyond the seas, the device of the Sinhalese was adopted by their conqueror, the great Raja Raja Chola, just as the fish of the Pandya and the bow of the Chera were adopted to proclaim that he was a Mummudi Chola, or the Chola with the three crowns? Coins too are not uncommon on which the legend 'Raja Raja' appears along with the Pandyan emblem, the fish, and the Chalukyan emblem, the boar. The former coin has on the reverse also the legend 'Sekhara' written twice. The two gold pieces in plate VI, of distinctly Sinhalese type with the legends Lankêsvara and Raja Raja, were probably issued by this ambitious monarch in Ceylon after his conquest of the Island. At a later age Lankapura Dandanadha issued the Kahapanas of Ceylon after humbling the Pandyas, thus, history having its tale of reprisals and repetitions.

Others there are attributable to this Chola king which bear distinctly Vaishnavite emblems such as the 'Vishnupāda', or feet of Vishnu, or the figure of Krishna as Muralidhara (the flute player,) familiar objects of worship among the Vaishnava sect. This fact is another instance of the king's religious toleration which made him endow a Buddhist monastery, and a Siva temple at about the same time.

In still other specimens bearing the legend Raja Raja, there is on the obverse the representation of a gallopping horseman, but the significance of this symbol it is not yet possible to definitely determine.

This diversity in the types of the coinage of Raja Raja tempts one to incline to the theory that the difference in type was the consequence of more than one prince of the same name having issued coins bearing the legend, Raja Raja. There was indeed more than one prince of the Chola kingdom bearing that name, but none so powerful or prosperous as the king who built the temple of Tanjore. It is therefore probable that the king when he conquered the Pandyas, ordered the fish emblems to be placed on the coins struck immediately after the victorious event, and a similar occasion might have prompted the adoption of the Chalukya and Simhalese devices, while the occurrence of Vaishnava and Saiva emblems alike on his issues serves to emphasize the extremely tolerant spirit that allowed of Vaishnava sculptures being wrought in the tower of the great Saiva Temple of Tanjore.

Rajendra succeeded his father Raja Raja in 1011 A.D. and vanquishing the Ganga prince after a sanguinary war, assumed the surname of Gangai Konda Chola. Like his father, he was ceaseless in activity in humbling his rivals and annexing their dominions and making the Chola rule steadfast from Kalinga in the north to Kumari in the south. He it was who probably built the temple and settled in the place called after him, Gagaikonda Cholapuram, in the Wodaiyarpalayam Taluk of the Trichinopoly District. Like his father he took delight in parading in his inscriptions what was very likely a fact that he had humbled the Pandyas and Cheras. During his reign another intermarriage with the Chalukyas of Vengi served to further cement the relationship first brought about by the marriage of Raja Raja's daughter to a Chalukya prince.

The coins of Gangai Konda Chola have the same devices both on the obverse and the reverse. 'In the centre is a seated tiger, the emblem of the Chola king, facing the right, with two fishes, the emblem of the Pandyan king in front, and a bow the emblem of the Chera king behind, the whole group flanked by two lamps and surmounted by a parasol and two chowries.' Underneath is the legend in Nagari 'Gangaikonda Chola' in two lines. The Collector of South Indian coins comes across now and then two other coins, one bearing the legend 'Sri Rajendra' and the other legend 'Uttama Chola' in Nagari characters both of the same type as the coins bearing the legend 'Gangaikonda Chola' already noticed. The first of these was evidently issued before the conquest of the Ganga country by Parakesari Varman, alias Rajendra Deva and the latter seems to have been issued when he assumed the surname Uttama Chola whenever that might have been. As already pointed out the title Uttama Chola was also assumed by Madurantaka, son of Gandaraditya, and the predecessor of Raja Raja.

In the first half of the eleventh century five kings ruled between the time of Gangaikonda Chola and that of Kulôttunga Chola who ascended the throne in A.D. 1070. They all recount in their inscriptions in high sounding terms their warlike exploits and conquests over the neighbouring kingdoms. But there is a blank in the coinage of this period and no coins of these five sovereigns have hitherto beer discovered.

In 1071 A.D. the daughter's son of Rajendra Chola, who was ruling from 1061 in Vengi or the Chalukya country usurped the Chola throne. He assumed the name, 'Kulôttunga Chola' and ruled over the southern country for nearly half a century. He had had been adopted by Rajendra alias Gangaikonda Chola as heir apparent to the throne, but only succeeded in obtaining the sovereignty by force in the year 1070 A.D., some nine years after he had become ruler of Vengi. The province of Vengi was thereafter entrusted by him to his uncle first, and then to his sons, one of whom Vira Chola assumed the office of Viceroy in 1078 A.D.

Kulôttunga I conquered the Kerala, Pandya, and Kuntala countries and was anointed in the Chola kingdom as Kulôttunga Chola Deva. It is not possible without encroaching much on the reader's time, to recount the doings of Kulôttunga during a long reign. One remarkable title of his however cannot be omitted. He was quite as just as he was valiant and being struck with the oppressive character of the numerous tolls and taxes till then levied and under the weight which his people were groaning, he abolished the tolls altogether thus gaining the name of Sungam tavirta Kulôttunga Chola Deva—he who abolished the tolls. Kulôttunga resided both at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Kanchipuram; the latter place which was only second in importance became a Chola city after the subversion of the Pallavas in the eighth century A.D.

One would expect that such a long reign could be illustrated by a fairly large variety of coins but the results of numismatic research till now have been disappointing. Some years ago there was a find of sixteen gold coins in the Krishna District, which are now in the Government Central Museum at Madras. The Government Epigraphist, to whom they were sent, deciphered and published them in the Indian Antiquary. The coin is described as follows:—'Centre: A boar facing the proper left and surrounded by two lamps, an elephant goad, a parasol, and two indistinct emblems.' Margin, Sri Raja Raja Samwat-34. 'The coins bear the legend on the obverse, while the punchmarks show through on the plain reverse. The irregular concave shape of the obverse was evidently caused by the gradual bending of the coin during the application of six several punches to make the impressions on the coins.'

In the same series have to be placed other coins which show on the obverse a boar and on the reverse the legend 'Chola Narayana.' The first of these is surmised by Dr. Hultsch to be that of Kulôttunga's father, the Eastern Chalukyan king, Raja Raja, who ruled between A.D. 1022-1063; while the latter is attributed to Kulôttunga himself from the fact that he had borne the surname, Rajanarayana. There are in my possession copper pieces which have on the obverse the standing figure, as in Raja Raja's coins, and on the reverse, a standing boar, with the Telugu or Canarese legend above, which may be read Cho and Nu. But unless better specimens are procured and further research throws more light on the coinage of this period, nothing definite can be stated about the reign in which the coin was issued.

The Chola power after Kulôttunga I, began gradually to wane and the last king with any pretentions to power was Kulôttunga III, 1278, A.D. By the year 1234, A.D. we see a Hoysala king established in the Chola country with his capital at Kannanore near Samayapuram. We hear also that Raja Raja III was captured by a Perum Singa and had to be rescued by a Hoysala king who consequently prided himself by assuming the title of the ' Establisher of the Chola Kingdom.' At this time too, the Pandyan power which had so long been subject to the Cholas, received a fresh impetus under Mara Varman Sundara Pandya who boasts of having burnt Tanjore and Uraiyur, presented the Chola kingdom to a favourite, but when the Chola prostrated at his feet made a free gift of the kingdom to him. Thus we find in the end of the thirteenth century, the Cholas decline and fall, after having for nearly four centuries been the sole arbiters of the destinies of Dravida Desam.

The coins belonging to this period of Chola sovereignty have not yet been found; but there are with me unassigned coins which possibly refer to the successors of Kulôttunga. On the obverse of all these is the standing Ceylon figure so often referred to above, while on the reverse is the figure of a standing bull, with the Nagari or Canarese syllable 'Vi' which may stand for 'Vikrama Chola', the immediate successor of Kulottunga alias Rajendra. It may not be improbable too that to the more than one Raja Raja that ruled after Kulôttunga we have to attribute the more modern looking of the copper issues bearing the legend Raja Raja.

Some of the Pandyan coins of this period throw light on the low ebb to which the Chola power had been reduced by various causes. One coin bears the legend 'Kachi Vaļangum Perumāl' which means that a Pandyan king after taking the Chola town Kanchipuram in battle, gave it back generously to the vanquished Chola prince.

The other records that the Pandyan king conquered the Chola country, in the brief legend “Chōnāđu Koṇdān.” Thus briefly is the story of the Chola coinage as far as it is known at present. By far the commonest of them are the copper cash of Rāja Rāja ; the gold and silver pieces are very difficult to obtain. The issues of a large number of the Chola sovereigns have yet to be discovered and deciphered. Vast quantities of these valuable store-houses of information are annually going ‘to the goldsmith’s crucible and the brazier’s melting pot’ and it is the duty of every earnest enquirer into the condition of Ancient India to rescue them from this cruel fate.

THE CHOLAS AND THEIR COINAGE

BY

DIWAN BAHADUR T. DESIKACHARI, B.A., B.L., M.R.A.S.

CENTURIES before the Christian era, the Cholas had established themselves on the coast of Coromandel (Chola mandalam) and enjoyed a civilization not less advanced than that of the Aryan Settlements in the North. They were referred to along with the Keralas and the Pandyas in the Second Rock Edict of the Buddhist Emperor, Asoka, in the third century B.C. The great chronicle of Ceylon, an ancient work in Pali called the Mahavanso, made it the theme of one of its main episodes, the war waged against the Island by the Chola Tamils in the early centuries preceding the Christian era.

Some scholars have advanced the hypothesis that it was a colony of Dravidian merchants who, becoming acquainted with an alphabetic writing derived from the white Pre-Semetic Akkadians north of the Euphrates Valley, brought the script to India, being thus the first to introduce the art of writing into Dravida Desam. There is in the proof that is adduced in support of this hypothesis much that tends to show that the Tamils, as early as the seventh century before the Christian era, had developed such a degree of maritime and commercial enterprise as to tempt them to undertake voyages across the sea to distant countries. The principal port of the Cholas was Kaveripaddinam, situated near the northern mouth of the Kaveri.
